passage:
Sunday night
A lesson in formatting, learnt the hard way. I'm organising the Lonavala trip for our batch, and this morning I sent the group one giant paragraph: dates, bus timing, what to pack, food, and at the end, "EVERYONE MUST CONFIRM BY FRIDAY!!! NO EXCUSES." Chandrika messaged me privately: "Nobody can find the bus time, and the capitals feel like you're yelling at us." I scrolled up and cringed. So I rewrote it:
- Dates: 14 and 15 December
- Bus: leaves the college gate at *6:30 a.m.*
- Bring: a warm jacket and a water bottle
- Please confirm by *Friday* so I can book seats
Line breaks, one bold time, one bold day, no capitals. Within an hour twenty-two people had replied with a thumbs-up, and two asked real questions instead of "wait what time??" Chandrika sent: "much better, less drill sergeant." I'll save capitals for real emergencies.
Jatin

qa.q: What time does the bus leave the college gate?
qa.a: At 6:30 a.m.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel on scrolling back up after Chandrika's message?
qa.a: Jatin cringed with embarrassment, seeing how the wall of text and the capitals came across.

qa.q: What made the rewritten message clearer?
qa.a: Separate lines for each detail, bold only on the key time and day, a polite reason for the deadline, and no shouting capitals.

qa.q: How did the first message feel to Chandrika and the batch?
qa.a: Hard to use, since nobody could find the bus time, and the capitals felt like being yelled at.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult using lists, line breaks and a little bold to make a message clear, after seeing that capitals and clutter felt aggressive.

passage: I'm Jahnavi, and last month my post on the college forum about hostel curfew timings blew up. Lokesh from the civil branch replied, "Typical. People who've never been fined lecturing the rest of us," and within an hour there were forty comments, half of them about me, not curfews. My fingers were shaking over the keyboard. I typed a reply full of capitals, then made myself close the laptop and walk around the hostel block. When I came back I didn't post in the thread. I messaged Lokesh directly: "I think we actually want similar things. Can we talk on a call instead of in comments?" Surprisingly, he agreed, and on the call he was calmer, even funny. But one anonymous account had started posting insults about my family. That I didn't engage with at all. I screenshotted every comment, reported the account to the forum moderators, and blocked it. The moderators removed it the next day.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi's post about?
qa.a: Hostel curfew timings.

qa.q: How was Jahnavi feeling while typing the first reply?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt angry and rattled, fingers shaking, ready to hit back in capitals.

qa.q: Which steps kept things from escalating?
qa.a: Closing the laptop and walking before replying, moving the talk with Lokesh to a private call, and screenshotting, reporting and blocking the abusive account.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have experienced Jahnavi's private message?
qa.a: As an unexpected olive branch, which may be why he agreed to talk and was calmer on the call.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult pausing before replying in a heated thread, moving to a private call, and screenshotting, reporting and blocking abuse.

subtype: Acting a role versus feeling it [Mismatch]
passage: I'm Kavitha, and in the drama society's winter play I played a mother whose son goes missing at a railway station. In the last scene I had to collapse on the platform bench and wail his name. Every night the hall went silent. On opening night my friend Lalremsiami came backstage with red eyes and hugged me. "Are you okay? That looked so real. Was it about your own family?" I laughed, a little guiltily. Honestly, during that scene I was counting. Three steps to the bench, drop on the fourth beat of the music, breathe from the stomach so the wail carries, and don't kneel on the loose nail at the edge of the stage. Inside I was focused, and a bit worried about that nail. The grief was on my face and in my voice because we'd rehearsed for six weeks, not because I was living it. Lalremsiami looked almost cheated. "So you're a very good liar." "No," I said. "A very good actor. Different thing."

qa.q: Where does the son go missing in the play?
qa.a: At a railway station.

qa.q: What was Kavitha actually feeling during the wailing scene?
qa.a: Kavitha felt focused, counting beats and steps, and a little worried about the loose nail, rather than grieving.

qa.q: What should an audience keep in mind after a performance like this?
qa.a: That visible emotion can be crafted through rehearsal, so the display is not proof of what the actor feels.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel on learning Kavitha had been counting beats?
qa.a: Almost cheated, having been so moved by grief that looked completely real.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult in a drama society showing convincing grief without feeling it, so a display should not be equated with the actor's own state.

subtype: Cultural performance and shared ritual arts [Expressing]
passage:
Monday: In the empty seminar hall, Hansa counted out the garba steps for the college fest team, clapping on each turn. Shreya, from Pune, kept speeding up and spinning as if it were a club dance. "Why do we all have to go round in a circle?" she asked, a little bored.
Wednesday: Hansa brought a small clay lamp and set it in the middle of the floor. "At home in Vadodara, during Navratri, we dance around the goddess's lamp. The circle is devotion, and it's also everyone together: aunties, kids, strangers." Shreya slowed down. "So I've been dancing at a party that's actually a prayer?" "Both, for lots of people," Hansa said. "Ask anyone what it means to them. You'll get different answers."
Saturday: On the fest stage, the lamp flickered in the centre. Shreya's steps matched Hansa's now, unhurried, eyes on the flame. Afterwards she said, "I felt part of something, not just performing it."

qa.q: Where is Hansa's home?
qa.a: Vadodara.

qa.q: Why do you think Hansa brought a clay lamp on Wednesday?
qa.a: Hansa likely felt it mattered for the team to understand the devotion and togetherness in garba, not just the steps, and chose patience over annoyance.

qa.q: What helped Shreya understand the garba?
qa.a: Asking about the circle, Hansa's explanation of the Navratri lamp, and the advice to ask people what it means to them.

qa.q: How did Shreya's experience of the dance change?
qa.a: From a bored, fast club-style spin on Monday to feeling "part of something" on the fest stage 🙂

grounding: It illustrates a young adult performing garba at a college fest to express devotion and community, and a learner asking about its context before judging.

passage:
Friday, after the screening
My short film finally played in the department auditorium tonight. Eleven minutes about Mola, my grandmother, making butter tea every morning in Dharamshala, the same way she did in Tibet. I meant it as quiet pride: she carried a whole home in her hands. In the Q&A, the first person said it was "so sad, so full of loss." Someone else called it "a film about hope." A lecturer said the long still shots felt "lonely." I wanted to argue with each of them. Then Shreya, who sat in the third row, told me afterwards that it made her call her grandfather in Patna for the first time in months. I hadn't made it for that. But it did that. I think I'm learning that once it's on the screen, it isn't only mine anymore. People bring their own grandparents into the room. My intent still matters. It just isn't the only thing that does.
Tenzin

qa.q: How long is Tenzin's short film?
qa.a: Eleven minutes.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel when people read the film as sad or lonely?
qa.a: Tenzin felt frustrated and wanted to argue, because the film was meant as quiet pride.

qa.q: What is Tenzin learning about sharing work with strangers?
qa.a: That audiences read work through their own experience, so the maker's intent matters but is not the only valid meaning.

qa.q: What did the film mean to Shreya?
qa.a: It moved her to call her grandfather in Patna for the first time in months.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult using film to share a viewpoint, and finding that strangers read it through their own experience, so intent and reception differ.

Pradeep: oh

qa.q: What is the series of paintings called?
qa.a: Monsoon Nights.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel on learning about the series?
qa.a: Pradeep felt a bit sheepish and humbled, having read the painter's mood from the colours alone.

qa.q: What can viewers fairly say about a painting, according to the chat?
qa.a: What it makes them feel and what is known about how the artist works, but not the maker's inner state.

qa.q: How had Jagdish once misread another artist?
qa.a: Jagdish assumed a painter was angry because of all the red, but he was copying old temple murals for practice.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult forming a view of an artist's mood from a painting and learning that craft, commission and tradition shape art as much as feeling.

subtype: Sculpture as expression of inner states [Expressing]
passage:
Sachin walked into the college ceramics studio and stopped in front of the shelf. "Whoa. Is this yours?"
"Yeah. Finished it last night," Darshan said, wiping clay off his wrists.
"Two hands gripping each other so hard the fingers are bending. It looks furious."
"Huh. For me it's my dad's hands. When his workshop closed, he held Ma's hand at the table and didn't say anything. I couldn't say anything either. So I made this."
"So it's sad?"
"Sad. Proud too. Those hands built that workshop over twenty years."
"I still see anger. Like the hands are fighting the whole world."
Darshan tilted his head and looked again. "Maybe there's some of that. I was angry at how it ended."
"Does it bother you that I read it differently?"
"No. You brought your own stuff. That's allowed."
Sachin ran a finger near the bent knuckles without touching them. "It's heavy. In a good way."

qa.q: For how many years did Darshan's dad build the workshop?
qa.a: Twenty years.

qa.q: What feelings did Darshan put into the sculpture?
qa.a: Sadness and pride about his father's closed workshop, and some anger at how it ended, feelings he couldn't say aloud.

qa.q: Why was it helpful that Darshan accepted Sachin's different reading?
qa.a: It let both meanings stand, and it even helped Darshan notice anger that had gone into the clay without being planned.

qa.q: How did Sachin read the sculpture?
qa.a: As furious hands fighting the whole world, a reading shaped by what Sachin brought to it.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult shaping clay to express feelings that are hard to say, and a viewer reading it differently, with both readings valid.

passage: The tattoo studio in Johannesburg smelled of antiseptic and incense. Zanele held out the old birthday card, "Sleep well, my child," in her late grandmother's looping handwriting. "Right here," she said, tapping the inside of her wrist. Kofi, who had come along for moral support, turned the card over. "It's beautiful. Can I ask two annoying questions? Your nursing placement starts in March. Will they mind it on your wrist? And will you still want it there at forty?" Zanele frowned. "It's my grandmother. Of course I will." Then she paused. "The wrist, though. I'll be washing my hands all day, right in front of patients." The artist suggested trying the words in henna first and living with them for a couple of weeks. Two weeks later Zanele came back. "The words stay. The place changes." The tattoo went on her upper arm, where she could show it when she chose. On the drive home she kept touching the bandage.

qa.q: What did the birthday card say?
qa.a: "Sleep well, my child."

qa.q: How did Zanele feel when Kofi asked the two questions?
qa.a: At first defensive about her grandmother, then thoughtful as she pictured herself at the nursing placement.

qa.q: How did Zanele think through the permanence?
qa.a: She tried the words in henna for two weeks, kept the meaning, and moved the tattoo to her upper arm to suit her work.

qa.q: What was Kofi trying to do by asking the questions?
qa.a: Kofi supported the tattoo but wanted Zanele to think about the placement and the future before choosing something permanent.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult choosing a tattoo as a personal marker while thinking through permanence and workplace norms.

passage:
Wednesday
Placement interviews today. I borrowed Didi's black blazer and ironed my one white shirt twice, because everyone says the first thirty seconds decide everything. In the waiting room most of us looked like a bank advert. Then Jagdish walked in wearing a faded kurta and rubber chappals, a cloth bag on his shoulder. I'll be honest: I thought, he's not serious, he won't get past round one. We ended up in the same group discussion. He spoke the least, but every time he did, the room changed direction. His point about delivery routes in hill towns was the best thing anyone said. Afterwards I found out his hostel had flooded and his only formal shirt was drying on a chair. He got shortlisted. So did I, thankfully. I'm glad I dressed with care; it helped me feel ready. But I judged a whole person by his chappals, and I was completely wrong.
Ira

qa.q: Why was Jagdish's formal shirt unavailable?
qa.a: His hostel had flooded and the shirt was drying on a chair.

qa.q: How did Ira feel after learning about Jagdish?
qa.a: Ira felt embarrassed and humbled at having judged him by his chappals.

qa.q: What balanced lesson does Ira take from the day?
qa.a: Dressing with care helped Ira feel ready and shows respect, but clothing is an unreliable measure of someone's ability.

qa.q: What might the day have been like for Jagdish?
qa.a: Probably stressful, arriving in a faded kurta after the flood among candidates in blazers, yet still speaking well enough to be shortlisted.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult dressing formally for an interview while learning that first impressions from clothing are unreliable measures of ability.
